title: The Isma'ilis
hookLine: a Shia community led today by a living Imam, the Aga Khan, known for development work

cards: What happens when a question comes up that nobody in the first centuries ever faced? A new medicine. A new kind of work.
A family that has moved to a country with different laws. Muslim communities have their own ways of answering. Some open the books of the schools.
Some ask a mufti. Some ask a marja'. One community turns to a living Imam, a descendant of the Prophet's family, whom they recognize as the guide for their own time.
His title is the Aga Khan. The community is the Isma'ilis.

teach.b: Isma'ilis are Shia Muslims who trace their line of Imams through Isma'il, a son of the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and they take their name from him. Twelver Shia followed a different son, which is where the two branches part.
The Isma'ilis described here hold that the line of Imams has never been broken, and that there is always a present Imam, the Imam of the time.
They point to a verse in surah al-Nisa, in Pickthall's words: "Obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority". For them, those in authority include the Imam.
Sunni scholars read the same words differently, as rulers or people of knowledge. Each reads it within its own tradition.
Isma'ilis gather in a jamatkhana, a house for the community's prayer and meeting. In South Asian communities, devotional songs called ginans are part of that life.
Isma'ilis speak of the outward form of faith and its inward meaning, and see the Imam as a guide to both. Then the work.
The Imam has built institutions grouped as the Aga Khan Development Network: schools, hospitals, rural support, care for historic buildings, help in places of poverty, open to people of every faith.
Isma'ilis explain this as faith that cares for life in this world as well as the next. Volunteering, giving time and skill, is woven through the community's life.

how: Isma'ili Muslims recognize a living Imam, the Aga Khan, as the guide of their time; they gather for prayer in a jamatkhana, and the community supports the Aga Khan Development Network's schools, hospitals and rural programs with volunteered time and giving.

games.q: you're an Isma'ili, and a question comes up that nobody faced in the first centuries. where does your community look for guidance?
o: only to the oldest books, never to anyone living.
to the living Imam, the Imam of the time.
to a vote of the whole community.
games.why: Isma'ilis hold that there is always a present Imam, and look to him as the guide for their own time.

practice: Bring to mind one place that served you without asking who you were, a school, a clinic, a library, a shelter, and one person who worked there. Stay with that picture for a few breaths and let gratitude be simple.
If you pray, thank Allah for that place in your own words.
